Tags: **[S]** primary public source, **[Y]** my synthesis, **[A]** simulation assumption. Data simulated.

## (a) Concept

| Topic | Idea |
|---|---|
| Reference interval (RI) | central 95% of a *healthy reference population*: 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, each with its own CI |
| Direct method | recruit and test healthy reference individuals (nonparametric percentiles) |
| Indirect method | mine routine patient data and statistically separate the healthy component (`refineR`) |
| Partitioning | separate RIs by sex/age if the groups differ enough to matter |
| Reference change value (RCV) | smallest difference between two serial results in one person that exceeds analytical + biological noise |
| Monitoring claim | evidence that *changes within a person* are measured reliably and mean something clinically: a **separate intended use** from a one-time diagnostic aid |

## (b) Regulatory anchor

| Item | Verified fact | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| EP28 | **EP28-A3c (Ed3), 2010-10-19, reaffirmed 2020-04**: protocol for defining, establishing and verifying reference intervals, incl. subject selection, preanalytical/analytical factors, calculation, transference | [S] clsi.org |
| Minimum n (the often-quoted 120 per partition) | *not verified: paywalled* | – |
| IVDR Annex I 9.1(b) | "expected values in normal and affected populations" is among the clinical-performance parameters | [S] |
| pTau217 label | The Roche 24 Aug 2026 release states the test is not intended as stand-alone and that safety and effectiveness are not established for predicting dementia or **monitoring** effect of therapeutic products; this appears in the release, not in the FDA decision summary text; labelling not seen | [S] ROCHE-0824 |
| FDA decision summary, cognitively normal reference interval | N = 167 (age 55-80): 95% reference interval 0.0832-0.628 pg/mL; 68.3% ≤ 0.223, 22.8% in 0.223-0.378, 8.98% > 0.378 (FDA-DS p.36; not re-checked by me) | [S] via notes |

## (c) R lab

### 1. Direct reference interval (nonparametric) with CIs

```{r ri}
set.seed(101)
n <- 240                                        # assumed >= 120 per partition is typical practice; EP28 text not verified
x <- rlnorm(n, log(1.0), 0.25)
np <- quantile(x, c(.025, .975), type = 6)
# CI 1: bootstrap percentile
bs <- boot(x, function(d, i) quantile(d[i], c(.025, .975), type = 6), R = 4000)
ci_boot <- rbind(boot.ci(bs, type = "perc", index = 1)$percent[4:5], boot.ci(bs, type = "perc", index = 2)$percent[4:5])
# CI 2: distribution-free order-statistic CI (binomial ranks)
rank_ci <- function(x, p, conf = 0.95) {
  n <- length(x); s <- sort(x)
  lo <- qbinom((1 - conf) / 2, n, p); hi <- qbinom(1 - (1 - conf) / 2, n, p) + 1
  c(s[max(lo, 1)], s[min(hi, n)])
}
ci_rank <- rbind(rank_ci(x, .025), rank_ci(x, .975))
true <- qlnorm(c(.025, .975), log(1), .25)
kable(data.frame(Limit = c("2.5th", "97.5th"), Estimate = np, `Bootstrap CI` = sprintf("%.3f - %.3f", ci_boot[, 1], ci_boot[, 2]),
                 `Order-statistic CI` = sprintf("%.3f - %.3f", ci_rank[, 1], ci_rank[, 2]), `True value` = true, check.names = FALSE),
      digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Two independent CI methods agree broadly; the upper-tail CI is much wider than the lower one because the tail is sparse and skewed. With n = 240, each limit rests on about 6 observations. [Y]

**Coverage check of the order-statistic CI** (1000 repeats):

```{r ri-cov}
set.seed(102)
cv <- replicate(1000, { z <- rlnorm(n, log(1), .25); r <- rank_ci(z, .975); true[2] >= r[1] && true[2] <= r[2] })
c(coverage_97.5th = mean(cv))
```

### 2. Indirect method with `refineR` on mixed routine data

3,000 routine results: 85% from healthy people (lognormal, same as above), 15% pathological with a shifted distribution.

```{r refiner}
set.seed(103)
h <- rlnorm(2550, log(1.0), 0.25); p <- rlnorm(450, log(2.0), 0.35); allx <- c(h, p)
cache <- "../cache/refiner_fit.rds"
if (file.exists(cache)) fit <- readRDS(cache) else { fit <- findRI(Data = allx, NBootstrap = 30, seed = 1); saveRDS(fit, cache) }
ri <- getRI(fit, RIperc = c(0.025, 0.975), CIprop = 0.95, pointEst = "fullDataEst")
kable(data.frame(Method = c("True healthy limits", "Naive percentiles of ALL data", "refineR (indirect)"),
                 `2.5th` = c(true[1], quantile(allx, .025), ri$PointEst[1]),
                 `97.5th` = c(true[2], quantile(allx, .975), ri$PointEst[2]), check.names = FALSE), digits = 3)
```

The naive upper limit is inflated by the pathological component; `refineR` recovers the healthy limits. It assumes the healthy component is (Box-Cox) normal and dominant; it replaces recruitment but does not replace judgement on population and preanalytics, and I make no claim that a regulator accepts it in place of EP28-style direct studies. [Y]

### 3. Reference change value from a mixed model

Log-scale model: `log y = subject mean + noise`. Analytical CV 4%, biological within-subject CV 8% [A], 150 stable subjects, 4 samples each.

```{r rcv}
set.seed(104)
ns <- 150; k <- 4
sd_b <- 0.30; sd_w <- sqrt(0.04^2 + 0.08^2)                        # log scale approximations of CVs
dd <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(ns), each = k))
dd$ly <- rnorm(ns, 0, sd_b)[dd$id] + rnorm(nrow(dd), 0, sd_w)
m <- lmer(ly ~ 1 + (1 | id), dd)
vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m)); s_w <- sqrt(vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"])
z <- qnorm(0.975)
rcv_model <- c(down = exp(-z * sqrt(2) * s_w) - 1, up = exp(z * sqrt(2) * s_w) - 1)
# second way: SD of paired differences of consecutive results
dif <- unlist(tapply(dd$ly, dd$id, function(v) diff(v)))
rcv_pairs <- c(down = exp(-z * sd(dif)) - 1, up = exp(z * sd(dif)) - 1)
# third: truth
rcv_true <- c(down = exp(-z * sqrt(2) * sd_w) - 1, up = exp(z * sqrt(2) * sd_w) - 1)
kable(rbind(`lmer within-subject SD` = rcv_model, `SD of paired differences` = rcv_pairs, `true (simulation)` = rcv_true) * 100,
      digits = 1, caption = "RCV (% change), two-sided 95%: RCV = exp(+-1.96 sqrt(2) SD_within) - 1")
# false-flag rate in stable people
nw <- 20000; a <- rnorm(nw, 0, sd_w); b <- rnorm(nw, 0, sd_w)
c(false_flag_rate = mean(b - a > log(1 + rcv_true["up"]) | b - a < log(1 + rcv_true["down"])))
```

The log-scale formula gives a slightly asymmetric interval (about −22% / +28% here). Detection of a *true* change: [Y]

```{r rcv-power}
set.seed(105)
sapply(c(0.20, 0.50, 1.00), function(ch) mean(rnorm(nw, log(1 + ch), sqrt(2) * sd_w) > log(1 + rcv_true["up"])))
```

(true increase of 20%, 50%, 100%: about 31%, 89% and 100% of individuals flagged). A genuine 20% rise is missed about two times in three: the RCV suits detection of large changes, not subtle ones. [Y]

### 4. Trajectory modelling: MMRM versus completers

Two-arm trial; change from baseline at months 6 and 12; unstructured covariance; control declines 1.0/2.0, drug 0.7/1.4 (true effect 0.6 at month 12); SD 2, correlation 0.6 [A].

```{r mmrm}
set.seed(106)
nper <- 150
sim_mmrm <- function(dropout = FALSE) {
  trt <- rep(0:1, each = nper); id <- seq_along(trt)
  S <- matrix(c(4, 2.4, 2.4, 4), 2)
  mu <- cbind(-1.0 + 0.3 * trt, -2.0 + 0.6 * trt)
  y <- mu + MASS::mvrnorm(length(trt), c(0, 0), S)
  miss12 <- if (dropout) rbinom(length(trt), 1, plogis(-1.2 - 0.9 * y[, 1] - 0.6 * trt)) == 1 else rep(FALSE, length(trt))
  data.frame(id = rep(id, 2), trt = rep(trt, 2), visit = factor(rep(c("6", "12"), each = length(trt)), levels = c("6", "12")),
             vnum = rep(1:2, each = length(trt)), chg = c(y[, 1], ifelse(miss12, NA, y[, 2])))
}
fit_mmrm <- function(d) {
  d <- d[order(d$id, d$vnum), ]; d <- d[!is.na(d$chg), ]
  f <- gls(chg ~ trt * visit, data = d, correlation = corSymm(form = ~ vnum | id), weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit),
           na.action = na.omit)
  b <- coef(f); c(`month 6` = b[["trt"]], `month 12` = b[["trt"]] + b[["trt:visit12"]])
}
d0 <- sim_mmrm(FALSE)
t12 <- with(d0[d0$visit == "12", ], mean(chg[trt == 1]) - mean(chg[trt == 0]))
kable(data.frame(Estimate = c("MMRM, complete data", "t-test difference, complete data"),
                 `Month 12 effect` = c(fit_mmrm(d0)[["month 12"]], t12)), digits = 4)
stopifnot(abs(fit_mmrm(d0)[["month 12"]] - t12) < 1e-6)
```

With balanced complete data, unstructured-covariance MMRM equals the per-visit mean difference (exact check above). With dropout related to earlier worsening (MAR), MMRM uses the month-6 data of dropouts; completers do not:

```{r mmrm-drop}
R <- 200
res <- t(replicate(R, { d <- sim_mmrm(TRUE)
  cc <- d[d$visit == "12" & !is.na(d$chg), ]
  c(MMRM = fit_mmrm(d)[["month 12"]], completers = mean(cc$chg[cc$trt == 1]) - mean(cc$chg[cc$trt == 0])) }))
kable(data.frame(Estimator = colnames(res), `Mean estimate (truth 0.6)` = colMeans(res), `Bias` = colMeans(res) - 0.6,
                 SD = apply(res, 2, sd), check.names = FALSE), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

### Why "monitoring" is a separate intended use [Y]

A diagnostic aid shows a result *discriminates* amyloid-positive from negative at one time. A monitoring claim needs: within-person precision and RCV in the target population (above), evidence the marker *changes* with treatment or disease course (responsiveness), evidence that changes relate to clinical or imaging change, stability of the assay over time and lots, and a defined action rule. None follows from AUC. That is why the Roche release states that effectiveness for monitoring is not established.

### Timed rehearsal: 30 random questions

Draw with `draw_questions()` (one per day at least), answer aloud in about 90 seconds each, score 0/1/2 (missed/partial/solid), then `score_rehearsal()` appends the misses to `flashcards.csv`.

```{r rehearsal}
#| results: asis
q <- read_questions("../interview_questions.csv")
drawn <- draw_questions(q, 30, seed = 2026)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(drawn))) {
  cat(sprintf("**%d. (Day %d)** %s\n\n", i, drawn$day[i], drawn$question[i]))
  cat('::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Model answer"}\n', gsub("\n", "\n", drawn$answer[i]), '\n:::\n\n', sep = "")
}
```

```r
# After the session (not run here): 30 scores, one per question in the order above
res <- score_rehearsal(drawn, scores = c(...), flashcards = "flashcards.csv")
res$pct; res$by_day; res$added
```
